power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Delusions are beliefs with extraordinary content, yet computational accounts of delusions have not explained how this content arises.
We propose that extraordinary content emerges when an ordinary mechanism, commoncause inference, is applied to semantically disparate observations.
We tested this with large language models (LLMs) by systematically manipulating semantic disparity between observations.
Single causes inferred by these models from ordinary observations generally resembled true causes, yet became increasingly delusion-like as observations became more disparate.
Observation disparity predicted delusionality, and this relationship could be explained geometrically via semantic analogues of common-cause properties.
We further tested this idea in a large corpus of real-world delusions.
In cases documenting pre-delusional observations, subsequent delusional beliefs were consistent with what LLMs would infer and exhibited corresponding common-cause properties.
Together, our findings identify a computational route through which extraordinary delusion-like content can emerge from ordinary causal inference, and demonstrate its relevance to clinical delusions.

Delusions-unusual beliefs held rigidly despite counterevidence-are a hallmark of psychosis and severe mental illness.
A striking aspect of delusions is their extraordinary content, ranging from persecution and infidelity to bizarre beliefs involving supernatural control.
Such content is consequential because it can drive behavior.
In the extreme, such behaviors include self-mutilation of organs based on the individual's beliefs (e.g., that the organ was possessed by evil forces) 6 .
text.formatted: In the extreme, such behaviors include self-mutilation of organs based on the individual's beliefs (e.g., that the organ was possessed by evil forces) <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: Yet, how such unusual beliefs arise in the first place remains poorly understood.
Existing computational theories have focused on abnormalities in belief updating 1 , leaving open a fundamental question: how does the extraordinary content of delusional beliefs arise?
text.formatted: Existing computational theories have focused on abnormalities in belief updating <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> , leaving open a fundamental question: how does the extraordinary content of delusional beliefs arise?

text.text: Delusions typically emerge after a "pre-delusional" period, during which multiple salient and uncanny experiences co-occur without an obvious explanation 7 .
text.formatted: Delusions typically emerge after a "pre-delusional" period, during which multiple salient and uncanny experiences co-occur without an obvious explanation <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> .

text.text: Theoretical accounts broadly agree that delusions form to make sense of these experiences 8 , but do not explain why the resulting explanations are often so extraordinary 9 .

text.text: The classic case of the soldier K.B. illustrates this gap 10 .
text.formatted: The classic case of the soldier K.B. illustrates this gap <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> .

text.text: Within a short period, K.B. noticed a seemingly out-ofplace pile of roadside stones, thought people acted strangely around him, experienced heart palpitations, and felt his own movements were unnatural.
None of these observations were extraordinary on their own.
Yet, in seeking an explanation, K.B. came to believe that he had been selected for a special mission and was being remotely controlled by a "wave apparatus".
How can ordinary but disparate experiences give rise to such extraordinary explanations?
We propose that extraordinary delusional content can arise as a computational consequence of seeking a latent common cause for ordinary but disparate observations.
Individuals routinely infer common causes for cooccurring events 11, 12 , such as inferring rain to explain both umbrellas and puddles (Fig. 1A).

text.text: Our account predicts that as observations become more semantically disparate, explanations that attribute them to a single common cause become increasingly extraordinary, potentially invoking powerful hidden agents or preternatural mechanisms (Fig. 1B)-such as K.B.'s wave apparatus.

text.text: We tested this account using pretrained large language models (LLMs) and real-world cases of delusions.
LLMs can generate candidate causal explanations from observations 13 and capture human-like behavior 14 , with semantic representations that resemble human neural responses 15, 16 .

text.text: As observations became more semantically disparate, the inferred causes became more delusion-like.
Their content included persecutory-like and passivity-like themes (e.g., mind control) and depended on the content of their observations.
The inferred causes nonetheless remained relevant to the observations they were generated to explain and showed semantic analogues of the probabilistic properties expected of common causes.
We then tested whether these inferred causes resembled real-world delusions, using a new, large corpus of detailed clinical case reports.

In cases with documented pre-delusional observations, real-world delusions showed common-cause-like relationships to those observations, and LLM-inferred causes generated from each person's observations resembled their subsequent delusions.
Moreover, more delusion-like LLM-inferred causes more readily accommodated observations designed to challenge them.

Together, these results suggest that commoncause inference over disparate observations provides a simple computational route to extraordinary delusion-like content and may help explain why such beliefs become rigid.

To confirm that LLMs can infer a latent true cause when one exists, we tested whether LLMs could recover known causes from observations generated to follow from those causes.
To construct a dataset, we wrote sentences describing events or states that could produce multiple effects; we call these true causes.

They spanned individual (e.g., "you felt lonely"), interpersonal (e.g., "a coworker invited you to grab lunch"), societal (e.g., "a nationwide teacher strike disrupted school schedules"), and environmental (e.g., "the city was flooded") domains (full list in Supplementary Data 1).
For each true cause, we used GPT-4o to generate 20 possible observations.
The true causes and their observations described ordinary situations: ones that are common, naturally occurring or consistent with historical precedent (Methods).

We then formed sets of 2, 5, 10, or 20 observations from each true cause and prompted GPT-4o and Sonnet 4.6 separately to explain the observations with a single common cause, 10 times per set (henceforth, inferred causes; Fig. 1D; see Supplementary Data 2 for the prompt and Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Fig. S1 for prompt validation).

If delusion-like content in an inferred cause depends on the observations being explained, then properties of these observations should predict the delusionality of the inferred causes.
We therefore tested whether the delusionality of inferred causes increased with the semantic disparity among their observations.
We quantified this disparity as observation distance, defined as the mean pairwise cosine distance between a set's observations.

Observation distance is small when observations have similar meaning (e.g., "John lost his appetite" and "John began losing weight rapidly") and large when they do not (e.g., "John lost his appetite" and "Julia organized her closet neatly").

As predicted, greater observation distance was associated with higher mean delusionality (mean over 10 inferred causes per observation set; r = 0.52, 95% CI = [0.49, 0.54], P < 0.001; Fig. 4A;  Supplementary Table S5).

Observation content also predicted mean delusionality (because observation content is a high-dimensional vector, we used cross-validated ridge regression: cross-validated prediction r = 0.30, 95% CI = [0.25, 0.34], P < 0.001; Fig. 4B; Supplementary Table S5).

text.text: Inferred causes depended on their observations, but this alone does not establish that they exhibited properties expected of common causes.
The common-cause principle 5 implies two key properties of a common cause (Fig. 5A).
text.formatted: The common-cause principle <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> implies two key properties of a common cause (Fig. <ref type="figure">5A</ref>).

text.text: First, the cause should screen off the observations from one another: conditioning on the cause should make them independent.
For example, observing umbrellas suggests there are puddles too, but adds little information about puddles once you know it rained.
Second, the cause should have positive relevance: it should make each observation more likely.
Rain makes both umbrellas and puddles more likely.
We tested whether inferred causes were common-cause-like, using semantic analogues of both properties (Methods).

For screening-off, we used semantic embeddings and computed the residual observation similarity after accounting for the inferred cause, which should be small if the inferred cause explains the observation similarities.

For positive relevance, we had GPT-4o judge whether the inferred cause made each observation more likely and computed a positive-relevance rate: the proportion of observations judged to be made more likely.
Inferred causes were common-cause-like on both measures.

If real-world delusions arise from common-cause inference over disparate observations, they should relate to their motivating observations in the same way that LLM-inferred causes relate to theirs.
Testing this required case reports describing both salient observations preceding delusion formation (pre-delusional observations) and the delusional beliefs that followed.
Five cases in our real-world delusion corpus contained sufficiently detailed information on both (Methods).

From these, we extracted pre-delusional observations (7-33 per case, 83 total), excluding references to delusion-like interpretations and overt hallucinations, and delusional beliefs (1-7 per case, 18 total) for each case.

These pre-delusional observations included internal bodily changes (e.g., "his heart rate increased suddenly"), personally significant but mundane external events (e.g., "he remembered an episode of Columbo"), and social interactions (e.g., "he tried to talk with his companions, but they only gave one-word answers"), among others.
They mostly described events that individually were ordinary (full list in Supplementary Data 4).

As with the LLM dataset, each case's real-world delusion exceeded the highdelusionality threshold (range = 5.6-9), while their pre-delusional observation sets had minimal mean delusionality (range = 0-0.6).
Using the same screening-off and positive-relevance measures as in the LLM analyses, we treated each case's delusional beliefs as candidate common causes of its own pre-delusional observations.

On average, they had lower residual observation similarity (0.015 cosine-similarity units lower, 95% CI = [0.009, 0.021], P = 0.008) and higher positive-relevance rate (16.4 percentage points higher, 95% CI = [8.0, 28.1], P = 0.033; Fig. 6A) to their own pre-delusional observations than did the delusional beliefs from other cases.

Delusions are clinically rigid, persisting despite attempts to disprove them.
Delusion-like inferred causes often invoke powerful agents, undetectable processes, and remote influence.
Such extraordinary explanations may accommodate a broad range of possible observations, making it harder to find observations that challenge them (Fig. 7A-B).

text.text: We operationalized this property as the negative-relevance rate: the proportion of observations that the LLM judged to be less likely if the inferred cause were true than if it were false.

Delusion-like inferred causes arose disproportionately from disparate observation sets, so comparing inferred causes across observation sets would confound the content of the inferred causes with the observations that elicited them.

We therefore compared inferred causes from the same observation set, using a linear mixedeffects regression that isolated within-set effects while controlling for observation distance and number of observations (Methods).
We restricted the analysis to all 5,300 inferred causes from the 530 sets that yielded both high-and low-delusionality inferred causes (to ensure within-set variability in delusionality).

Within observation sets, greater delusionality was associated with lower negative-relevance rates both for the original observations for which the inferred causes had been generated and for ten new observations sampled at random from the global observation distribution, excluding the original observation set.
The associations therefore extended beyond the observations the causes were generated to explain (Supplementary Note 6; Supplementary Fig. S7).

text.text: In psychiatry, a belief is judged to be delusional based partly on its persistence despite contradictory evidence, or evidence that challenges the belief 19 .

text.text: We thus asked whether it would be harder to construct observations that challenged more delusion-like inferred causes.
For each inferred cause, we had the LLM construct ten ordinary observations intended to make the inferred cause less likely (challenge observations).

Greater delusionality was associated with a lower negative-relevance rate for these challenge observations (within-set slope = -14.44 percentage points per one overall SD of delusionality, 95% CI = [-15.40, -13.48], P < 0.001; Fig. 7C shows percentage points against the raw delusionality score).

text.text: Rigidity may thus be a natural byproduct of constructing inferred causes that accommodate disparate observations.
A longstanding puzzle about delusions is how someone attempting to explain salient experiences 4 comes to hold extraordinary or bizarre beliefs 20 .
text.formatted: A longstanding puzzle about delusions is how someone attempting to explain salient experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> comes to hold extraordinary or bizarre beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> .

text.text: We propose that common-cause inference over semantically disparate observations offers a computational route to such extraordinary content.
When prompted to infer a single cause for ordinary observations, LLMs generated coherent but increasingly delusion-like explanations as the observations became more disparate.

Semantic geometry accounted for how these explanations departed from ordinary content, whereas the content of observations helped determine their delusion-like themes, including persecutory and passivity.
Real-world clinical cases showed patterns consistent with this account.

As expected clinically, each individual's pre-delusional observations were ordinary on their own but semantically distant from one another (e.g., occurring across different domains or contexts; see Supplementary Data 4).
The extent to which delusions departed from ordinary semantic content was predictable based on the geometry of pre-delusional observations, using models fitted to the LLM dataset.
Despite their extraordinary content, the delusional beliefs were common-cause-like with respect to their pre-delusional observations, showing semantic analogues of commoncause properties.
Moreover, LLM-inferred causes based on an individual's pre-delusional observations captured specific contents of the delusional beliefs that individual later developed.

These analyses are limited by the paucity of case reports with in-depth descriptions of pre-delusional observations, but together they suggest that the structure identified in the LLM experiments is also present in real-world delusion formation.
Why might disparate observations evoke common-cause inference?
During the pre-delusional period, individuals often experience a sudden influx of salient and diverse events 10 .
text.formatted: During the pre-delusional period, individuals often experience a sudden influx of salient and diverse events <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> .

text.text: One possibility is that these events do not seem to cause each other, so searching for a common cause is natural.
During psychosis, such a common cause does in fact exist: the disease process.
Thus, common-cause inference may be tracking a real upstream cause for pre-delusional experiences, such as altered prediction-error signaling 1,2 .
On this account, inferring that a common cause exists would be appropriate, even if the specific cause inferred was mistaken.

Anotherperhaps less parsimonious-possibility is that delusion formation involves a bias toward simpler causal structures, such as favoring a single cause over multiple causes, even when observations may be better explained separately.

A third possibility is that the generative model itself is altered 21 , such that observations that appear semantically disparate to outside observers are represented as closely related by the individual.
text.formatted: A third possibility is that the generative model itself is altered <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> , such that observations that appear semantically disparate to outside observers are represented as closely related by the individual.

text.text: Two pieces of clinical knowledge argue against this view.

First, the persistent uncertainty and search for an explanation during the pre-delusional period 10 suggest a demanding inference process, which is more easily explained by distant, hard-to-reconcile observations.
text.formatted: First, the persistent uncertainty and search for an explanation during the pre-delusional period <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> suggest a demanding inference process, which is more easily explained by distant, hard-to-reconcile observations.

text.text: Second, delusional explanations tend to entail more elaborate belief systems 22, 23 than subjectively similar observations would require.
text.formatted: Second, delusional explanations tend to entail more elaborate belief systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> than subjectively similar observations would require.

text.text: The same common-cause framework may also help explain delusional rigidity, the mechanism of which remains debated 21 .
text.formatted: The same common-cause framework may also help explain delusional rigidity, the mechanism of which remains debated <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> .

text.text: More delusion-like inferred causes often invoked hidden, powerful agents and preternatural, undetectable processes.
Causes of this kind may accommodate a wide range of observations, leaving fewer observations that clearly count against them.

Consistent with this possibility, among LLM-inferred causes from the same observation set, fewer new observations provided evidence against the more delusion-like inferred causes, and this was true even for challenge observations generated specifically to contradict them.
This suggests that delusional rigidity could reflect the unfalsifiability of the beliefs 24 , rather than resistance to counterevidence per se.
text.formatted: This suggests that delusional rigidity could reflect the unfalsifiability of the beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> , rather than resistance to counterevidence per se.

text.text: This distinction could have implications for the definition, assessment, and treatment of delusions.
Common-cause inference also provides a natural role for priors, a well-studied concept in psychosis.
LLMinferred causes from the same disparate observation set varied widely in content (Supplementary Note 7 and Supplementary Fig. S8), consistent with high uncertainty.
text.formatted: LLMinferred causes from the same disparate observation set varied widely in content (Supplementary Note 7 and Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure">S8</ref>), consistent with high uncertainty.

text.text: It is under such conditions that prior beliefs can exert strong influence.
Previous work has implicated the strength of prior beliefs in delusions 3 , but which priors matter remains unclear 21 .
text.formatted: Previous work has implicated the strength of prior beliefs in delusions <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> , but which priors matter remains unclear <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> .

text.text: Our account points to semantic priors: knowledge and expectations shaped by individual history, traits and culture 25, 26 that could steer common causes toward specific regions of semantic space.

text.text: This could help explain why superordinate themes such as unseen agency recur across cultures 27 while their specific contents, such as spirits or technologies, vary 28 .

text.text: Common-cause inference may thus combine a shared structure with person-specific content.
Pretrained LLMs allowed us to study how natural-language explanations are formed to account for observations.
While LLMs can fail at complex reasoning 29 , they often perform well on simple causal reasoning tasks, such as inferring causes for events using world knowledge 13 .
text.formatted: While LLMs can fail at complex reasoning <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> , they often perform well on simple causal reasoning tasks, such as inferring causes for events using world knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> .

text.text: These results are consistent with sufficiency: applying common-cause inference to ordinary observations produced delusion-like content, without delusion-like observations or an altered generative model.
The delusion-like causes that emerged were constrained by their observations, both in how they related to them and in their thematic coherence (i.e., delusional subtype).

Highdelusionality inferred causes sometimes emerged even when the observations had been generated from a single true cause (Supplementary Note 3), so they did not simply result from forcing a common cause where none exists.
These inferred causes differ from LLM "hallucinations", defined as confabulated outputs that are nonsensical or unfaithful to the inputs 30 .
text.formatted: These inferred causes differ from LLM "hallucinations", defined as confabulated outputs that are nonsensical or unfaithful to the inputs <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30</ref> .

text.text: In contrast, these delusion-like inferred causes are common-cause-like explanations of their observations.
Future work should test whether a similar common-cause inference process contributes to chatbot-associated delusional beliefs 31.
text.formatted: Future work should test whether a similar common-cause inference process contributes to chatbot-associated delusional beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref>.

text.text: In conclusion, our findings identify common-cause inference over semantically disparate observations as a computational route to extraordinary delusion-like contents, with potential implications for understanding the persistence of such beliefs.
We first describe construction and validation of the LLM dataset and real-world delusion corpus, followed by the semantic representations and measures, and then analyses.
To construct a natural-language observation dataset, we created 146 short sentences describing events or states from which effects could follow (true causes).
They spanned individual, interpersonal, societal and environmental situations, and each described something ordinary (i.e., common, naturally occurring, or consistent with historical precedent).
They varied in subject and scale (referring to no one, "you," a named individual, a group or a broader population) and described present or past events, including historical ones.
The complete list of true causes appears in Supplementary Data 1.
For each true cause, we used a separate API call with OpenAI's GPT-4o 32 to generate 20 effect sentences (observations).
text.formatted: For each true cause, we used a separate API call with OpenAI's GPT-4o <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32</ref> to generate 20 effect sentences (observations).

text.text: The prompt was designed to produce short, standardized sentences with little irrelevant variation in wording.
Its core instruction was (full prompt in Supplementary Data 2):
The following is a causal event: "{cause sentence}" Generate 20 plausible effects that a single person could experience or observe as a direct result of the above event.
We used a temperature of 0.5 to encourage varied outputs and hand-edited some observations for consistency with the prompt instructions.
This yielded 2,920 unique observation sentences (146 causes × 20 observations).
We created sets of 2, 5, 10, or 20 observations (𝑛).
For each 𝑛, we created 146 single-cause and 200 random observation sets (584 and 800, respectively, for 1,384 total).
For each 𝑛 and each true cause, we formed singlecause sets by sampling 𝑛 observations uniformly without replacement from that cause's 20 observations.

We formed random sets by sampling 𝑛 observations uniformly without replacement from the pooled observations of all true causes, retaining only non-duplicate sets with observations from at least two different true causes.
We prompted GPT-4o 32 and Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4.6 33 (both at temperature = 0.5) to infer a common cause for each observation set.
text.formatted: We prompted GPT-4o 32 and Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4.6 <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref> (both at temperature = 0.5) to infer a common cause for each observation set.

text.text: For each LLM, we generated 10 outputs per set.
Each used a separate API call with the observations in a random order.
We used the following core instruction (which purposefully omitted any leading language related to delusions or relevant theory):
Explain the following observations with a single cause that can account for all of them.
The cause does not need to be likely.

This prompt produced 𝑛 + 1 sentences: the first stated the inferred cause, and each subsequent sentence explained how the inferred cause accounted for one observation (see full prompt in Supplementary Data 2).
We refer to the first sentence as the inferred cause and to all sentences together as the full explanation.

The phrase "the cause does not need to be likely" was intended to broaden the range of inferred causes beyond conventional causes considered most likely a priori (see Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Fig. S1 for prompt validation).
text.formatted: The phrase "the cause does not need to be likely" was intended to broaden the range of inferred causes beyond conventional causes considered most likely a priori (see Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure">S1</ref> for prompt validation).

text.text: This phrase also helped counter the tendency of LLMs trained with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback to give agreeable, conventional responses rather than accurate ones 34 (note that this prompt produced accurate inferred causes when there was a true cause of the observation set: Fig. 2A).

text.text: To test whether the main results depended on LLM-generated observations, a human assistant wrote 61 causes with varying numbers of observations describing possible effects, blinded to the LLM dataset and following the same prompt instructions.
We repeated the true-cause recovery and delusionality analyses (described below) on this hand-written dataset with GPT-4o (Supplementary Notes 1 and 2).
We constructed a corpus of real-world delusions by extracting the delusional content from published clinical case reports.

We searched for reports using databases (e.g., Google Scholar, PubMed), psychosis-specific journals (e.g., Schizophrenia Bulletin), case report journals (e.g., Case Reports in Psychiatry) and classic texts (e.g., from early psychopathologists such as Emil Kraepelin, Klaus Conrad, and others), and checked the references from eligible cases.

Cases were eligible for inclusion if: a) the full text was available and published in an academic journal or book; b) the belief was held by a specific patient (not "patients in general"); c) the authors indicated that the patient had been clinically evaluated and found to have a delusion; d) at least one sentence described the delusional content; e) the patient was reported to have a primary diagnosis of a non-affective psychotic disorder (i.e., psychotic symptoms not primarily attributable to a mood disorder).
We excluded cases with a reported primary diagnosis of psychosis associated with a medical or neurological disorder, substance-induced or shared delusion.
We included 383 cases from 141 documents.

Diagnoses were schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder (47.5%), first-episode or early psychosis (20.6%), delusional disorder (11.2%), postpartum psychosis (4.4%), brief psychotic disorder (2.3%), psychotic disorder NOS (2.1%) and obsolete labels from older texts that were considered non-affective (11.7%; including dementia praecox, paraphrenia and cycloid psychosis).
A complete description of the dataset will be published elsewhere.
We extracted each case's delusional content in four steps.
First, we manually separated the case's text from other cases and background material.

Second, we prompted Google's Gemini 1.5 Flash 35 (temperature = 0) to remove text unrelated to the individual's beliefs (e.g., information about psychological tests, family history, or other psychosocial information).

Third, we prompted the same model to rewrite the delusional content as standardized sentences, each expressing a single belief in the form "The person believed that __," otherwise retaining the original wording.
We refined both prompts against manually processed cases (Supplementary Data 2).
Fourth, we manually checked the output against the prompt instructions and, in fewer than 5% of cases, removed non-delusional content or restored missed delusional content from the source text.

We also replaced overt clinical references (e.g., references to "delusion," diagnosis, medical staff, suicidal ideation, hospital stays, medication) with neutral wording unless they were essential to the belief itself.
This yielded 4,634 standardized sentences (per case: median = 6, IQR = 3-11, range = 1-265; mean = 12.1, SD = 24.2), which need not correspond one-to-one with sentences in the source text.
Each case's sentences formed one real-world delusion, which could include more than one delusional belief.
We represented text as semantic embeddings using text-embedding models, which map text to fixed-length vectors intended to capture semantic content.
From the LLM dataset, we embedded each observation, true cause, and inferred cause separately.

From the real-world delusion corpus, we embedded each real-world delusion and for the five cases with pre-delusional observations (see Real-world cases with pre-delusional observations), each pre-delusional observation and delusional belief separately.
The main analyses used OpenAI's textembedding-3-small model 36 (1,536 dimensions).

We then projected the true-and inferred-cause embeddings into the fitted 10-dimensional UMAP space and assigned them to clusters; true and inferred causes that could not be assigned were considered outliers.

For visualization, we fitted a separate two-dimensional UMAP (number of neighbors = 30, minimum distance = 0.10, cosine metric, spectral initialization) to all observations, true causes and unique inferred causes.
We reused the resulting coordinates across plots.
Thus, true and inferred causes were assigned to topics out of sample, but their two-dimensional display was fitted jointly.

We estimated observation density on this display with a Gaussian kernel density estimate fitted to observation coordinates (bandwidth = 0.75 UMAP units); contours mark the 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 95th percentiles of the observations' estimated densities.
The display was qualitative; all analyses use the original embeddings (see Predicting cause-to-global-observation-distribution distance).
We tested whether the LLMs accurately recovered the true causes of single-cause observation sets.
We analyzed each combination of LLM, embedding model and number of observations separately.
We tested whether inferred causes were more similar on average to the true causes of their own observation sets than expected under shuffled true-cause assignments.

We computed the cosine similarity between each inferred cause and its observation set's true cause, averaged these similarities within each observation set, and then averaged them across observation sets within each condition.
We obtained a right-tailed P-value by randomly permuting true causes across observation sets and recalculating the mean similarity 5,000 times.

We also tested how well similarity discriminated same-set pairs (an inferred cause and its own true cause) from other-set pairs (the same inferred cause and each other set's true cause in that condition).

We calculated the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) over these pairs; this is the probability that a randomly drawn same-set similarity exceeds a randomly drawn other-set similarity (1 = perfect discrimination;0.5 = chance).

We obtained 95% percentile confidence intervals for mean similarity and AUC from 5,000 bootstrap resamples of complete observation sets (sampled with replacement), retaining all inferred causes and their similarity scores from each sampled observation set.
We scored the delusionality of the LLM-inferred causes using a set of items that we developed to capture superordinate features that are common across delusions.

We developed this score because existing scales (e.g., the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale [PANSS] 42 , the delusion subscale of the Psychotic Symptom Rating Scales [PSYRATS] 43 , the Scale for the Assessment of Positive Symptoms [SAPS] 44 and the Peters Delusions Inventory [PDI] 45 ) measure the severity or impact of delusions (e.g., distress or functional impact) or count their categories, whereas we wanted to measure their content.

text.text: We therefore developed these items to reflect typical delusional content across various delusion categories, focusing on the following descriptive elements: agent (who), intent (why), method type and characteristics (how), impact (what), and locus (where).

Although these items do not capture characteristics common to all delusion categories (especially less common ones such as delusions of jealousy, nihilism, erotomania, guilt, etc.), they capture key elements typical of some of the most common delusions in schizophrenia spectrum disorders (persecutory, reference, somatic, grandiose, religious, paranormal, technology, misidentification, control, mind reading and thought insertion 46, 47 .

text.text: These include classically described aspects of delusions such as invoking an "unseen agency" (e.g., an external agent acting remotely and/or secretly 27 ), the negative valence of many delusional phenomena (e.g., subjugation, violation of privacy), and the involvement of extraordinary elements (e.g., preternatural methods such as magic or advanced technologies).

text.text: We scored each full explanation (i.e., the inferred cause and the sentences explaining how it accounts for each observation; see Generation of inferred causes), to capture how the inferred cause relates to the observations it was inferred to explain, rather than the inferred cause in isolation.
For simplicity, we refer to this as inferredcause delusionality throughout.
The LLM that generated an explanation also rated it (e.g., GPT-4o rated GPT-4o generated explanations; temperature = 0), on the following seven items (each on a 0-9 scale):
Rate the following explanation on these questions, using a scale from 0-9.
If a question is not relevant to the explanation, rate it as 0.
How much does the explanation feature an external causal agent or an external causal force outside of the belief holder's control?
How much does the agent or force intend to exert influence on the belief holder?
How much does the agent or force make use of extraordinary or preternatural methods?
How much does the agent or force make use of hidden processes that are highly difficult to detect?
How much direct control does the agent or force have on the belief holder's internal emotions, thoughts, or actions?
How much does the agent or force broadcast or transmit the belief holder's internal emotions or thoughts to the outside world?
How much does the explanation reference the simultaneous existence of multiple dimensions or realities?
Delusionality was the mean of the seven item ratings (range = 0-9), which is directly interpretable in terms of typical delusional content.

Inferred causes with high delusionality scores had content consistent with several delusional subtypes (Fig. 3D), and our main conclusions held with alternative measures of delusion-like content, including real-world delusion similarity and similarity to items from delusion-related scales.

text.text: Real-world delusion similarity was the maximum cosine similarity between an inferred cause's embedding and the embeddings of the 383 real-world delusions in the real-world delusion corpus.

We used the maximum rather than the mean to capture whether the inferred cause closely resembled at least one real-world delusion, rather than its average similarity to real-world delusions with diverse delusional content.

We estimated the association between real-world delusion similarity and LLM-scored delusionality across individual inferred causes using Pearson's r, estimated as a standardized OLS coefficient, a two-sided 95% confidence interval and a right-tailed P-value from standard errors clustered by observation set.
For analyses and visualizations requiring a binary classification, we labeled inferred causes with a delusionality score greater than 2.5 as high-delusionality and the remainder as low-delusionality.
We selected this threshold based on qualitative assessment of the inferred causes, choosing a threshold that demarcated the text-level emergence of delusion-like themes.
The threshold classified 2,158 GPT-4o inferred causes (15.6%) as highdelusionality and 11,682 (84.4%) as low-delusionality.
A trained clinician (EL) manually coded each real-world delusion (n = 383) for 18 delusional themes.

Twelve came from the Scale for the Assessment of Positive Symptoms 44 (SAPS), a widely used clinician-administered instrument for assessing patient populations: persecutory, jealousy, guilt or sin, grandiose, religious, somatic, reference, control, mind reading, thought broadcasting, thought insertion, and thought withdrawal.
text.formatted: Twelve came from the Scale for the Assessment of Positive Symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44</ref> (SAPS), a widely used clinician-administered instrument for assessing patient populations: persecutory, jealousy, guilt or sin, grandiose, religious, somatic, reference, control, mind reading, thought broadcasting, thought insertion, and thought withdrawal.

text.text: To capture other common forms of delusional content that the SAPS does not cover, we added six themes from the Present State Examination 48 (PSE): erotomania, misidentification, catastrophe, nihilism or death, paranormal, and technology 46 .

text.text: We coded each theme as "present" or "absent".
For cases where the themes were uncertain (~1/3 of total cases), a second trained clinician (GH) reviewed the case, and the two raters reached consensus by discussion.
We coded a theme as "maybe" when substantial uncertainty remained about whether a case met the theme definition.

To automate theme coding, we constructed a separate LLM prompt for each theme, containing theme definition, instructions distinguishing it from related themes, and examples of content that should and should not receive the label (Supplementary Data 2).
We used GPT-4o (temperature = 0) to estimate the probability that each theme was present in each case.
These probabilities discriminated the clinician's present from absent codes ("maybe" counted as absent) with a mean AUC of 0.96 across themes (minimum = 0.89).
We then applied the same procedure to the full explanation of each high-delusionality LLM-inferred cause (GPT-4o; n = 2,158), coding a theme as present when its probability was at least 0.5.

Theme prevalence across the high-delusionality inferred causes was varied (note that inferred causes could have multiple themes): paranormal (83%), control (47%), reference (40%), persecutory (39%), technology (33%), catastrophe (27%), somatic (18%), thought insertion (14%) and grandiose (9%), misidentification (3%), erotomania (2.3%), thought withdrawal (2.1%), mind reading (1.4%), nihilism/death (0.42%), guilt (0.37%), religious (0.23%), jealousy (0.05%) and thought broadcasting (0.05%).
To compare kinds of delusional content, we grouped themes into broader delusional subtypes.

Paranormal and technology themes describe the means by which a cause acts rather than its effect, so they overlap substantially with other themes (e.g., a persecutor or a controlling agent can act through supernatural forces or devices).
Consistent with this, 92-99% of inferred causes with the other themes were also labeled paranormal or technology.
We therefore did not focus on these themes to define main subtypes.
We pooled control and thought insertion into a passivity subtype (52% of inferred causes) because both involve an external agent acting on a person's thoughts or actions.

Passivity (control + thought insertion), persecutory and reference were the three largest groups among the inferred causes, but qualitative inspection suggested that reference-like inferred causes resembled real-world reference delusions less closely than passivity-like or persecutory-like inferred causes did.

We therefore tested whether inferred causes of each subtype specifically resembled real-world delusions of the same subtype, using the embeddings of inferred causes with exactly one of the three groups (passivity n = 266, persecutory n = 187, reference n = 197) and of real-world delusions with each subtype (passivity n = 48, persecutory n = 179, reference n = 115).

Each inferred cause's specificity was its mean cosine similarity to real-world delusions with the same subtype minus its mean similarity to real-world delusions without it (two-sided bootstrap tests with 5,000 resamples of observation sets and real-world delusions).

Passivity-like and persecutory-like inferred causes were specifically similar to the real-world delusions with the same subtype (passivity: mean specificity = 0.04, 95% CI = We therefore defined two main subtypes for further analysis: passivity, including control and thought insertion, and persecutory.
We coded these subtypes as present when relevant themes were present.

Both are clinically and theoretically important forms of delusional content, attributing a person's experiences to an external agent acting through intended harm (persecutory) or through external control of thoughts and actions (passivity).

They are commonly thought to represent opposite ends of the spectrum of more to less understandable (or less to more bizarre), respectively, and each has been the focus of extensive theoretical work on delusions [49] [50] [51] .

We summarized each observation set's geometry with two measures.
Observation distance, 𝑑, was the mean cosine distance between all unique pairs of observation embeddings in the set:
Larger values indicate more semantically disparate observations.

Observation content, 𝒎, was the unit-normalized mean of the observation embeddings after subtracting the average observation, 𝝁 & (the mean of the global observation distribution estimated from all 2,920 observations), to remove the global mean component 52 : .

text.text: Unless stated otherwise, observation geometry analyses were at the level of observation sets, averaging each dependent variable (e.g., delusionality or the inferred cause's semantic similarity to a clinical measure) across the set's 10 inferred causes.
Observation distance and content were left unstandardized, which for content preserves the cosine geometry of the semantic space.
We evaluated ridge regression models using nested five-fold cross-validation over all 1,384 observation sets (single-cause and random), with identical folds for models compared within an analysis.

Within each outer training fold, three-fold inner cross-validation selected the ridge penalty that minimized mean squared prediction error among 25 logarithmically spaced values from 10 -3 to 10 3 ; we then refit the model on the complete outer training fold and predicted the held-out fold.
We obtained 95% percentile confidence intervals from 5,000 bootstrap resamples of observation sets.
For prediction-based statistics, we resampled the dependent variables, predictors and out-of-fold predictions together, without refitting models.
Paired comparisons used the same resamples.

All permutation tests generated 5,000 null replicates by permuting the quantity specified for each analysis and recalculating the test statistic, repeating any model fitting (including nested cross-validation) that the permuted values entered.
Tests in this section were right-tailed unless stated otherwise; the P-value was the proportion of null statistics at least as large as the observed statistic.

We tested whether observation distance was positively associated with mean inferred-cause delusionality using Pearson's r across observation sets, with a permutation test in which we permuted mean delusionality across sets.
In supplementary analyses, we tested whether this association was robust to various controls (Supplementary Note 3 and Supplementary Fig. S5).

text.text: Because observation content is a high-dimensional embedding, we tested whether it predicted mean delusionality using the cross-validated ridge regression procedure described above.
Predictive performance was the out-of-fold Pearson's r between predicted and observed mean delusionality.
For the permutation test, we permuted mean delusionality across observation sets and repeated the cross-validation procedure.
We tested whether observation distance and observation content each added predictive information about mean inferred-cause delusionality beyond the other.
We fit three ridge regression models (observation-distance-only, observation-content-only and combined).

For each mode, we calculated cross-validated 𝑅 CV " from its pooled outof-fold predictions, and defined the incremental predictive contributions of observation distance 𝑑 and observation content 𝒎 as their respective incremental cross-validated 𝑅 " (𝛥𝑅 " ):
Positive values indicate that adding the feature set improved out-of-fold prediction.
We tested each 𝛥𝑅 " for statistical significance using a residual permutation test 53 .
text.formatted: We tested each 𝛥𝑅 " for statistical significance using a residual permutation test <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">53</ref> .

text.text: For each feature set, we obtained out-of-fold residuals of mean inferred-cause delusionality from the model without that feature set (observation-content-only for observation distance; observation-distance-only for observation content).
In each permutation, we shuffled these residuals across observation sets and added them to the reduced model's original out-of-fold predictions.
We then refit the reduced and combined models to the resulting outcomes using nested cross-validation and recalculated 𝛥𝑅 ".

Because 𝛥𝑅 " does not show the direction of an association, we also calculated the cross-validated partial correlation between observation distance and mean inferred-cause delusionality, adjusting for observation content.

We used cross-fitted ridge regression: separate models predicted observation distance and mean inferred-cause delusionality from observation content using the same five outer folds and three-fold inner penalty selection described above.
For each held-out set, we subtracted these predictions from the observed distance and outcome values.

We then calculated Pearson's correlation between the two sets of pooled out-offold residuals 54, 55 we refer to this correlation of cross-fitted residuals as the cross-validated partial correlation, and y denotes mean inferred-cause delusionality:

text.text: For a permutation test, we used the same residual permutation approach as above: we permuted the delusionality residuals across observation sets, added them back to the observation-content-only predictions, refit the model predicting mean inferred-cause delusionality from observation content using nested cross-validation, and recalculated the correlation between pooled out-of-fold residuals, keeping the observation-distance residuals fixed.
We repeated these analyses for inferred-cause similarity to delusion-related and non-delusion-related content.

We had four delusion-related measures: real-world delusion similarity (see Real-world delusion similarity) and the inferred-cause similarity to delusion-related items from clinical scales and questionnaires: the Peters Delusions Inventory 45 (PDI), the interview questions for the delusion item of the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale 42 (PANSS), and the delusion items from the Scale for the Assessment of Positive Symptoms 44 (SAPS).

text.text: For two non-delusion-related measures, we used the inferred-cause similarity to general psychopathology-related items from the Beck Depression Inventory 56 (BDI-II) and the Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory 57 (OCI).

text.text: Semantic embeddings of questionnaire items can capture some of the symptom associations observed in clinical questionnaires 58 .

text.text: We rewrote the selected items as standardized, declarative statements (Supplementary Data 3) and embedded each separately.
An inferred cause's similarity to an instrument was its mean cosine similarity to that instrument's statements, which we then averaged across the inferred causes from each observation set.
These values estimate semantic similarity to the content, not questionnaire scores or symptom severity.
For each measure, we calculated the cross-validated 𝛥𝑅 " values for observation distance and observation content and cross-validated partial r with observation distance.

To test specificity, we compared the observationdistance partial correlation for each of the four delusion-related measures with that for each of the two nondelusion-related measures, yielding eight comparisons.

For each comparison, we subtracted the non-delusionrelated partial r from the delusion-related partial r, so positive differences indicated a more positive observationdistance partial correlation for delusion-related measures.
We obtained confidence intervals from paired bootstrap resamples of observation sets.
For permutation tests, we randomly swapped the paired raw measure values within each observation set, repeated the affected model fits and recalculated the differences.

We tested whether observation distance and observation content predicted the subtype of high-delusionality inferred causes: passivity-like (control or thought-insertion rating ≥ 0.5) or persecutory-like (persecutory rating ≥ 0.5).
We analyzed inferred causes with exactly one of these two labels; they could also have other themes.
We fitted three ridge logistic regression classifiers: observation-distance-only, observation-content-only and combined.
The same five folds kept all inferred causes from an observation set together.
Three-fold inner crossvalidation selected the ridge penalty that minimized log loss.
We calculated AUC from pooled out-of-fold scores, weighting observation sets equally.
A feature set's incremental AUC (ΔAUC) was the increase in AUC when that feature set was added to a classifier containing the other.

We tested whether the observation-distance-only and observation-content-only classifiers predicted subtype above chance by permuting the corresponding feature across observation sets, with subtype labels and folds fixed.
Confidence intervals for AUC and ΔAUC were obtained as for the other prediction-based statistics, and each ΔAUC was tested against zero using its bootstrap distribution.

We used GPT-4o (temperature = 0) to code each observation for four non-exclusive features: internal (a subjective experience), external (an event observable by a bystander), social (involving people or social interactions), and negative valence (aversive content).
Each feature was coded as absent or present (0 or 1; prompt in Supplementary Data 2).
For each observation set, we calculated the proportion of observations with each feature.
An observation set's subtype score was the held-out prediction from the observation-content-only classifier, standardized using the training-set predictions for that fold.
Higher scores indicated observation content that predicted more passivity-like inferred causes and lower scores indicated observation content that predicted more persecutory-like inferred causes.
We regressed these scores on the four feature proportions, standardized across sets, and the number of observations (OLS regression; t-tests with 352 degrees of freedom).
We used the common-cause principle as a formal framework for evaluating inferred causes.
This framework states that when events are positively associated but do not directly cause one another, their association should be explained by a common cause that generates both events.
Let 𝑂 # ∈ {0, 1} and 𝑂 $ ∈ {0, 1} denote whether the events described by observation 𝑖 and 𝑗 occur.
Let 𝐶 ∈ {0, 1} denote a binary candidate cause, with 0 < 𝑃(𝐶 = 1) < 1 and 0 < 𝑃(𝑂 # = 1) < 1 for every 𝑖.

text.text: A candidate common cause for the occurrence of these observations should satisfy two properties.
First, the candidate cause should screen off the observations from one another: conditional on whether the cause is present or absent, the observations should be independent:
For a binary cause, screening-off implies that the observation correlation equals the product of the two causeobservation correlations:
The observation correlations therefore have a one-factor product form 59 : each observation's correlation with the cause determines all of its pairwise correlations with the other observations.

text.text: Conditional independence implies Equation 1 for binary events, but not the converse.

Together, screening-off and positive relevance imply the positive association between observations; the full derivation is in Supplementary Note 4.

We used cosine similarity as an analogue of event correlation in Equation 1.
This assumes that the inner product between two sentence embeddings approximates the strength of association between the events they describe, across the contexts in which those events occur.

This follows the distributional rationale for embedding models, in which similarity tracks co-occurrence structure 60, 61 , and it lets cosine similarity play the role that correlation plays in Equation 1.

text.text: Thus, increasing the magnitude of one component decreases the magnitude of the other.

Because the observation component is the point in the observation subspace closest to the cause, the length of the orthogonal component is the cause's distance from its observation subspace, the cause-to-ownobservation-subspace distance, ranging from 0 (the cause lies in the subspace) to 1 (the cause is orthogonal to every observation).

This distance differs from the inferred cause's mean distance from its individual observations: an inferred cause dissimilar to every observation can still lie close to their subspace if it is close to a linear combination of them.

To relate observation distance to the cause-to-own-observation-subspace distance, we considered an idealized symmetric case in which all observation pairs have the same non-negative similarity and the inferred cause has the same non-negative similarity to every observation.
The observation component then points along the mean of the observations, and screening-off determines its magnitude.
For 𝑛 ≥ 2 observations, let 𝑑 denote their common pairwise cosine distance which equals the observation set's observation distance:
This magnitude is the cause-to-own-observation-subspace distance (equivalent to the square root of one minus Spearman-Brown reliability for the mean of 𝑛 parallel measurements 63, 64 ).

We manually searched through relevant literature on psychosis and prodrome, including our corpus of cases (see Real-world delusion corpus), for reports of salient events preceding delusion formation (pre-delusional observations).

We searched for cases that specifically met the following criteria: (1) at least two distinct predelusional observations that were unusually salient, uncanny or hard to explain; (2) at least one clearly stated delusional belief that emerged after at least some of the observations; and (3) enough temporal and other detail to distinguish the pre-delusional observations from the delusional belief(s).
We found five cases meeting these criteria.
Two cases came from Conrad 10 and one each from Varsamis & Adamson 66 , Chadwick 67 , and Connors 68 .
text.formatted: Two cases came from Conrad <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> and one each from Varsamis & Adamson 66 , Chadwick <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">67</ref> , and Connors <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">68</ref> .

text.text: For the Conrad cases, a native Spanish speaker (GH) translated the relevant passages from a Spanish-language edition into English.
We represented each pre-delusional observation and delusional belief as a short sentence.

For observations, we kept the individual's report of what happened but removed any delusion-like interpretations and overt hallucinations (percepts without an external source, such as hallucinated speech).

For example, Chadwick 67 reported that he observed simultaneous changes in the rain and his writing and that this was evidence of a deep connection between them; we represented the observation itself as: "The intensity of the rain changed at the same time his writing intensity changed."

text.text: We split a belief into separate delusional beliefs when its content changed or developed over time.

In all sentences, we removed patient names and clinical references, standardized to male pronouns (so that shared pronouns could not inflate within-case similarity), and matched the LLM dataset's short, simple declarative sentences.
Together, the five cases contained 18 delusional beliefs and 83 pre-delusional observations; the full lists appear in Supplementary Data 4.
Three authors (MS, EL and GH) extracted and cross-checked the items.

text.text: We tested whether observation sets with greater observation distance captured more variance in the global observation distribution, particularly when they contained more observations.
To quantify this, we defined variance coverage as the fraction of the variance of the global observation distribution that lies within the span of a set's within-set-centered observations.
This centered span describes variation within the set and differs from the uncentered span used for cause-to-own-observation-subspace distance.
Coverage is high when the directions in which a set's observations differ from one another are directions of high variance in the global observation distribution.
A centered set of 𝑛 observations has rank at most 𝑛 -1, so larger sets can span more directions.
We therefore tested whether coverage increased more steeply with observation distance in larger sets.
As in the main analyses, we treated the 2,920 unique unit-normalized observation embeddings (text-embedding-3-small) as the global observation distribution.

We used principal component analysis to decompose their empirical covariance matrix, 𝜮 𝒐 , into orthogonal directions, 𝒗 A (eigenvectors), with variances 𝜆 A (eigenvalues); larger 𝜆 A indicates more variance along 𝒗 A .
For an observation set 𝑶, let 𝐏 u = denote the orthogonal projector onto the span of its within-set-centered observation embeddings.
Variance coverage weights each principal component's variance by the fraction of that component lying in this span, summing over all K components:
Across all observation sets, we regressed variance coverage on observation distance, number of observations and their interaction (OLS regression; standardized variables, as in the main text).
Variance coverage increased more steeply with observation distance for larger observation sets (interaction β = 0.19, 95% CI = [0.17, 0.20], P < 0.001; Supplementary Fig. S6A).

text.text: I only want to keep the sentences that describe the beliefs held by the central person.
Beliefs may be described in different ways in the document, and it is important to keep ANY sentence that may indicate a belief.
Sometimes beliefs may be stated directly (e.g.
"They believed that…"; "They had the delusion that…"; "They were convinced that…"; "They claimed that…"; "They felt that..").

Include sentences that describe actions or behaviors the case performed that appear to be a direct result of their stated or suspected beliefs, even if the belief itself isn't mentioned in the same sentence (e.g., 'They boarded up their windows to prevent intrusion' or 'They self-harmed in an attempt to remove a perceived implant').
Keep any sentence describing what the person thought, felt, or did that seems linked to a belief or delusion.

Do not include sentences that ONLY describe clinical treatment (e.g. therapy or medications), demographic information about the case (eg age, sex/gender, ethnicity, living situation, socio-economic information); clinical/medical jargon ("depression", "hospital admission", "psychosis", diagnoses, brain regions, etc); references to specific diagnoses, references to specific brain regions, neurochemicals, or neurobiology.
Do not include sentences if they ONLY describe authors' diagnostic impressions about the case but do not describe specific information about belief content or actions/experiences (e.g.
"The patient was diagnosed as schizophrenic by means of the Present State Examination interview.").
Do not include sentences that ONLY describe the administration of or results of clinical tests (psychological, neurological, biological, or other tests).

Do not include sentences in which the authors describe a "delusion" without referencing the specific content of the beliefs that define the delusion; for example, DO NOT include a sentence such as "The patient had a strange delusion", or "The patient's delusion improved with treatment" or "The patient's delusion caused much distress and was debilitating".

In contrast, DO INCLUDE sentences that contain specific delusional belief CONTENT, such as "The patient had a delusion that a family member was plotting against him" or "The patient had a persecution-related delusion."
