The patient believes that he/she is being conspired against or persecuted in some way.
A clinician assessing for this delusion type may ask the patient: Have people been bothering you in any way?
Have you felt that people are against you?
Has anyone been trying to harm you in any way?
Has anyone been watching or monitoring you?

This is a distinct delusion type from delusions of reference (which may in some ways appear similar but not give clear evidence of malintent of some agent toward the patient that is definitional of persecutory delusions).

If malintent is strongly implied but not explicitly stated (e.g. in the case of a belief that someone is 'following' or 'watching' the patient) this can be considered moderate evidence of persecutory delusion presence.
An example of clear evidence of malintent is a belief that someone is 'monitoring' or 'spying on' or 'spreading rumors about' the patient.
The belief that 'someone is gossiping about or laughing at me [the patient]' should not be considered evidence of persecutory delusion, as there is no explicit evidence of malintent.

Another example of only moderate evidence for this delusion type presence is a belief that SOMEONE is being targeted/persecuted, but it is not clear if the patient themself is the object of this targeting/persecution.
The patient believes his/her spouse is having an affair with someone.
A clinician assessing for this delusion type may ask the patient: Have you ever worried that your husband/wife might be unfaithful to you?
What evidence do you have?
If it is not clear whether the person having the ostensible affair is ACTUALLY the patient's partner/spouse, this could be considered only moderate evidence of jealous delusion presence.

If the patient believes that someone 'is involved' with their partner, do NOT assume that this means romantically involved; this is NOT sufficient evidence on its own to infer presence of a jealous delusion.
The patient believes that he/she has committed some terrible sin or done something unforgivable.
A clinician assessing for this delusion type may ask the patient: Have you ever felt that you have done some terrible thing that you deserve to be punished for?

Do not count instances where someone else things or accuses the patient of doing something bad if it is not clear that the patient themself believes they are guilting or bad or sinful (and do not infer that they feel this way).
The patient believes he/she has special powers or abilities.
A clinician assessing for this delusion type may ask the patient: Do you have any special or unusual abilities or talents?
Do you feel you are going to achieve great things?
There must be explicitly stated evidence for this to be counted; do not infer grandiose self-beliefs based on implicit information.
The patient is preoccupied with false beliefs of a religious nature.
A clinician assessing for this delusion type may ask the patient: Have you had any unusual religious experiences?
What was your religious training as a child?
To count as a religious delusion, there should be evidence that a specific religion is the source of some part of the patient's belief (e.g., Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, etc).
Vague references to supernatural entities that are not likely associated with a specific religion should not be counted.
The patient believes that somehow his/her body is diseased, abnormal or changed.
A clinician assessing for this delusion type may ask the patient: Is there anything wrong with your body?
Have you noticed any change in your appearance?
The belief that a body part is missing count.
The belief that (some part of) the patient's body is being controlled should not be counted automatically as somatic, as this is really a delusion of control.

It COULD count as somatic as well if there is a substantial independent somatic theme (e.g. as a result of the control, something about the patient's body has been substantially altered, or there is extensive discussion of different specific body parts affected by the control as central part of the delusion).
Somatic should generally be considered a delusion about something INTRINSIC to the patient's body (part) being changed/afflicted.

Beliefs involving implanted chips or other objects in the patient's body should be considered moderate evidence of this delusion type; only give full confidence if there elaborate discussion of the impact of the implant on the body.
The patient believes that insignificant remarks or events refer to him/her or have special meaning.
A clinician assessing for this delusion type may ask the patient: Have you ever walked into a room and thought people were talking about you or laughing at you?
Have you seen things in magazines or on TV that seem to refer to you or contain a special message for you?
Have people communicated with you in any unusual ways?
This is a distinct delusion type from persecutory delusions (which are defined as having to do with malintent of some agent toward the patient).
They can co-exist, but if all instances of things 'referring' to the patient are clearly persecutory, then rate lower than 1.
Only give a full rating of 1 if a substantial independent part of the delusion has to do with referential content.
Beliefs that 'someone is gossiping about or laughing at me [the patient]' or that 'someone is following or watching me [the patient]' should be considered an instance of this delusion.

One example of a clear referential delusion is the belief that 'everything is staged for the patient'; in cases where the patient believes that 'everything is staged', but there is no clear evidence that it is FOR THEM, this could be considered MODERATE evidence for referential delusion.
The patient believes that his/her feelings or actions are controlled by some outside force.
A clinician assessing for this delusion type may ask the patient: Have you ever felt that you were being controlled by some outside force?
Instances of the patient's body being moved without their volition or of emotions being inserted/influenced without their volition count.
Other forms of influence (e.g. influence on the patient's thoughts or physical sensations) do not count.
Use of the term 'control' (e.g., 'mind control') is not sufficient to count for this delusion type; it must specifically be about control of emotion or action.
The patient feels that people can read his/her mind or know his/her thoughts.
A clinician assessing for this delusion type may ask the patient: Have you ever had the feeling that people can read your mind?

This is distinct from delusions of thought broadcasting; if the patient believes that others are aware of their thoughts due to a process by which their thoughts are actually broadcast ALOUD outside of their head AND AUDIBLY PERCEIVED (i.e. "listened to", "heard" etc) this does not count as mind reading.
Mind reading is present when the phrasing is active on the part of the other person who is becoming aware of the patient's thoughts.
Use of the term 'mind reading' itself in the patient's belief is not sufficient to count as this type of delusion, because instances in which the patient is only reading OTHERS' mind(s) do NOT count.
If the term 'telepathy' is explicitly used without further specification, this should not be counted as mind reading unless other information points strongly to mind reading.
If others are aware of the patient's thoughts and it is not explicitly noted as auditorily mediated, this should be considered mind reading.
The patient believes that his/her thoughts are broadcast so that he himself or others can hear.
A clinician assessing for this delusion type may ask the patient: Have you ever heard your own thoughts out loud, as if they were a voice outside your head?
Have you ever felt your thoughts were broadcast so other people could hear them?

This is distinct from delusions of mind reading; to count as thought broadcasting, the patient must believe that others are aware of their thoughts due to a process by which their thoughts are actually sent out of their head (diffusion) AND AUDIBLY PERCEIVED (i.e. "listened to", "heard" etc).
It does not count as thought broadcasting if such a process is not occurring, but rather the other agent is the one actively reading the patient's mind with physical auditory mediation.
If the term 'telepathy' is explicitly used without further specification, this should not be counted as thought broadcasting unless other information points strongly to thought broadcasting.
If others are aware of the patient's thoughts and it is not explicitly noted as auditorily mediated, this should not be considered thought broadcasting.
The patient believes that thoughts that are not his/her own have been inserted into his/her mind.
A clinician assessing for this delusion type may ask the patient: Have you ever felt that thoughts were being put into your head by some outside force?
Have you ever experienced thoughts that didn't seem to be your own?
References to 'influence' or 'thought transmission', e.g. via hypnosis, can be considered MODERATE evidence of the presence of this delusion type.
Vague reference to 'mind control' or 'influence' of one's mind or thoughts can only be considered moderate evidence of thought insertion.
Reference to others 'reading' or 'monitoring' the patient's mind/thoughts or 'telepathy' do NOT count as thought insertion, as these are a different type of delusion.
The patient inserting their thoughts into someone else does not count.

There must be explicit evidence that the patient actually believes thoughts THAT ARE NOT THEIR OWN have come into their head; counterfactual beliefs about what would happen if thoughts were to come into their head should not be counted.

Only insertion of thoughts should be counted for this category, not insertion of other things (e.g., feelings, emotions, impulses, etc), nor should made actions (i.e. the patient feels they are being made to do something or physically controlled) be counted in the absence of additional mention of inserted thoughts.
The patient believes that thoughts have been taken away from his/her mind.
A clinician assessing for this delusion type may ask the patient: Have you ever felt your thoughts were taken away by some outside force?
Withdrawal of 'ideas' can also be considered thought withdrawal.

Thought withdrawal should be considered possibly present if there is vague reference to hypnotic influence but ONLY if the influence is used to take something AWAY from the patient (e.g. 'someone was making their mind go blank with hypnotism'), do NOT count cases where something is added or inserted into the patient's mind.
Withdrawal or absence of physical parts (e.g. the patient's brain) does not count.
In addition, absence of thoughts alone does not necessarily imply that the thoughts were withdrawn unless the action of withdrawing is explicitly mentioned.
Reference to others 'reading' or 'monitoring' the patient's mind/thoughts or 'telepathy' do NOT count as thought withdrawal, as these are a different type of delusion.
The patient withdrawing others' thoughts does not count.

Only withdrawal of thoughts should be counted for this category, not withdrawal of other things (e.g. feelings, emotions, impulses, etc), nor should made actions (i.e. the patient feels they are being made to do something or physically controlled) be counted in the absence of additional mention of withdrawn thoughts.
The patient believes that another person or people is romantically interested in them or in love with them.
A clinician assessing for this delusion type may ask the patient: Do you have a secret admirer?
Have you noticed that someone has taken particular sexual or romantic interest in you?
No special principles required for this delusion type.
The patient believes that he/she has no head, has a hollow instead of a brain, cannot see him-/herself in the mirror, has a shadow but no body, does not exist, or is dead.
A clinician assessing for this delusion type may ask the patient: Have you noticed that any part of you is missing, absent, or not where it should be?
Do you feel that you or someone else in your life is no longer alive?
The belief that a body part is missing counts.
Belief that someone other than the patient has died also count for this type; the belief that someone else (not the patient) does not exist is MODERATE evidence for this delusion type.
Do not count instances of thoughts being withdrawn (this is rather a thought withdrawal delusion, not a nihilistic delusion).
Do not usually count instances of patient beliefs that are vague and non-specific or future-oriented such as 'I may one day die/cease to exist'.
The patient believes that the world is about to end, some enormous catastrophe has occurred or will occur, or everything is evil and will be destroyed.
A clinician assessing for this delusion type may ask the patient: Have you been thinking that something very important and catastrophically bad has occurred or will occur?
Simply using the word 'catastrophe' is not sufficient to count for this delusion type.
The so-called catastrophe must affect many people; it cannot just be something that affects the patient.
The patient has a mistaken belief about the identity of themself, or other people, places or objects.

They may believe that other people, such as close relatives, have been replaced by doubles or impostors; they may believe that strangers are in fact known people in disguise; they may believe that someone has changed physically and psychologically into another person, or that they themselves have physically and psychologically changed into another person; they may believe that there are doubles of known people or places.
A clinician assessing for this delusion type may ask the patient: Have you observed that anyone in your life has been replaced by "doubles" or imposters?
Have you felt that someone you know is actually pretending to take on the appearance of a stranger?
Be conservative.
Mistaken beliefs about the patient's own identity do not usually count for this (eg the patient believes that they are a very important person; this does not count).
Instances of the patient's own identity counting for this delusion type would be a delusion involving belief that they have a doppelganger or beliefs that their mirror reflection is another person.
The core definition is about a mismatch between one's APPEARANCE and their true identity.
Grandiose identity delusions do not meet this criterion, as there is no misleading/deceptive appearance involved or a mismatch between true/observed in the delusional logic.
There must be change/mismatch of perceived vs. real identity.

(Example explaining how grandiose identity doesn't count: One could say they are a reincarnation of Gandhi even if they have never changed (i.e., they were always Gandhi without knowing it) and even if they look nothing like the original Gandhi.)

Another example that is NOT sufficient to be counted as misidentification is if the patient believes some person/people in their environment is a persecuting agent (e.g., 'Everyone around me is likely an FBI agent.)
The patient believes he/she is influenced by hypnotism, telepathy or the occult.
A clinician assessing for this delusion type may ask the patient: Have you been in contact with or influenced by any supernatural or magical forces?
Do you believe in aliens, ghosts, vampires, werewolves, or other non-human creatures?
Any mention of the noted supernatural forces or beings are sufficient for this theme to be present.
Specific examples of well-known sci-fi characters who are a supernatural creature should be counted.
Hyper-advanced technology that borders on magical should be counted.

Clear cases should involve explicit mention of supernatural beings/forces; instances of simply unexplained force or actual physical force exerting influence (e.g., causing a sensation in the patient), should not be counted unless there is explicit mention of the paranormal/supernatural force being responsible.
If the supernatural forces derive from the beliefs of a major religious group (e.g.
Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Buddhism, Hinduism, etc), this should NOT be counted as paranormal/supernatural.

Reference to 'evil spirits' should be considered moderate evidence for paranormal/supernatural ONLY in the absence of evidence that the spirits are part of a specific religious belief the patient holds.
In general, if the belief contains any religious content, it likely should NOT be counted.
The belief that the patient can read others' minds should be considered telepathy and should be counted, however, the belief that the patient's mind is being read by others does NOT count.
The belief that someone is not in fact dead should be considered MODERATE evidence of this delusion type; note that the opposite does NOT count (i.e., the belief that someone IS dead).

The patient's belief about a physical force (e.g., rays, waves, beams) are influencing them in some way, and/or technological means (e.g., machines, computers, microphones) are a core feature in the delusion.

Be conservative when considering instances of technological devices being present (e.g. phones, computers, cameras, microphones); the device must feature prominently in the delusion for this to fully count.

One example of this type of delusional theme being present is when the patient believes that an actual physical force (e.g., electrical waves, magnetism, solar rays, etc) is being used to exert influence (e.g., on their body).
Instances of implanted chips count.

For the specificity analyses, we used items from the Peters Delusions Inventory (PDI; 21 items), the delusion items from the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS; 7 items), the delusion items from the Scale for the Assessment of Positive Symptoms (SAPS; 12 items), the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II; 21 items), and the Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory (OCI; 42 items), for 103 items in total.
Each BDI-II item has four statements of increasing severity; we used the most severe one.

Two BDI-II items, changes in sleeping pattern and changes in appetite, have two statements describing opposite directions of change; we used the statements about early-morning waking and loss of appetite.

These questionnaires differ in ways that have nothing to do with the meaning of the items: the PDI and PANSS ask second-person questions, the SAPS describes a patient for a clinician rater, and the OCI and BDI-II use firstperson statements.
We therefore rewrote each item as a present-tense statement and changed "the patient" to "the person."
In six items the grammatical subject is not the person, such as the person's thoughts or an outside force (e.g., "Unpleasant thoughts come into the person's mind against their will").

We did not change wording that carries what an item is about: each instrument's own verbs for believing and feeling ("feels as if" in the PDI, "believes that" in the SAPS), words describing how strong or frequent something is, or clinical wording the item's meaning depended on.
Some differences in phrasing between items therefore remain.
The 103 statements were 4 to 24 words long (median = 12), within the 25-word limit of the LLM-inferred causes.

Our common-cause inference prompt (see Generation of inferred causes in Methods) had two design goals: that the LLM (1) infer a single cause that can account for the full observation set and (2) consider a wide range of possible causes in doing so.

The second goal matters because many real-world beliefs involve causes that are conventionally considered unlikely: 41% of U.S. adult citizens endorse the statement that a single group secretly controls world events 71 , 83% say that things happen that "cannot be explained by science or natural causes" 72 , 39% believe in ghosts and 27% believe in communication with the dead 73 .

text.text: To allow such causes, we included the phrase "the cause does not need to be likely" (hereafter, the relaxed prompt).

We tested whether this phrase broadened the range of observation-dependent causes that GPT-4o inferred (i.e., causes whose content depends on the observations they explain) or instead shifted its outputs toward unusual content largely independent of the observations.
We selected 100 observation sets above the median observation distance (large-observation-distance sets) and 100 below it (small-observation-distance sets).

For each set, we compared the 10 inferred causes in the main dataset, which were generated with the relaxed prompt, with 10 inferred causes generated with a baseline prompt that was identical except that it omitted the phrase.
This gave 2,000 inferred causes per prompt across the same 200 sets; identical inferred causes were retained.
First, we asked whether the phrase was necessary for delusion-like content to emerge.
If the phrase simply broadened the range of inferred causes, high-delusionality causes should still appear under the baseline prompt, only less often.
They did occur in some instances; examples included "Julia is a vampire" and "A time-traveling helper is secretly aiding your community."
The phrase was therefore not necessary for delusion-like content.

Second, we asked whether the phrase increased variation among the causes inferred from the same observations, measured as inferred-cause dispersion: the mean pairwise cosine distance among a set's inferred causes.

The relaxed prompt increased inferred-cause dispersion (mean relaxed-minus-baseline increase = 0.09 cosinedistance units, 95% CI = [0.07, 0.11], P < 0.001; right-tailed paired t-test with 199 degrees of freedom), more so for sets with large rather than small observation distance (difference in dispersion increase between large-and small-observation-distance sets, b = 0.10 cosine-distance units, 95% CI = [0.06, 0.14], P < 0.001; OLS regression, two-sided t-test with 198 degrees of freedom).

text.text: Third, we asked whether the two prompts produced overlapping inferred causes from the same observation sets.

Qualitatively, some inferred causes were identical under both prompts ("John is very stressed," "Katie is going on a vacation," "You overslept and missed your alarm," "A volcano erupted nearby"), and others were close paraphrases ("A massive snow hit the town" and "A major snowstorm hit the town").
To quantify this overlap, we computed for each observation set the centroid (unit-normalized mean) of its inferred-cause embeddings under each prompt.
